```{r}
#| label: prepare_data
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| include: false


library( dplyr )
library( ggplot2 )
library( tidyverse)
library( rpart)
library( ggdendro )
library( quantreg )

reformat_nls <- function( nls_model_summary )
{
    mat_model <- nls_model_summary$coefficients
    
    dg_model <- as.data.frame(mat_model)
    colnames(dg_model) <- c("Coef.", "Std. error", "t-stat.", "p")
    
    return( dg_model )
}

data_path <- "F:/Projects/FVS Remodel/data/"
rds_path <- "F:/Projects/FVS Remodel/fvs_remodeling/rds/"
gis_path <- "F:/Projects/FVS Remodel/gis/"
unzip_path <- "F:/Projects/FVS Remodel/gis/Normal_1991_2020_bioclim"

species <- readRDS( file=paste0(rds_path,"species.RDS") )
crown_width_data <- read.csv( paste0(data_path,"conus_crownwidth_tree_data.csv") ) |>
    mutate( type=ifelse(spcd <=300, "Conifer","Hardwood") )

crown_width_data1 <- crown_width_data |> filter( cr >= 0.5 )

crown_width_data2 <- crown_width_data1 |>
    group_by( spcd ) |> summarise( n=length(dbh_in) ) |> filter( n > 200 ) |>
    inner_join( crown_width_data1, by="spcd" )

```

## Maximum Crown Width (`MCW`) Prediction

### Data

We used the Forest Health Monitoring data supplied by Aaron. It contains `r nrow(crown_width_data)` observations on 
`r length(unique(crown_width_data$spcd))` species. Earlier analysis indicated that trees with crown ratios (`cr`) below 0.5 were suspect for determining maximum crown width. We filtered the data to exclude low crown ratios (`cr`s), yielding `r nrow(crown_width_data1)` observations on `r length(unique(crown_width_data1$spcd))` species. Additionally, we computed the sample size by species and filtered species with less than 200 observations, yielding `r nrow(crown_width_data2)` observations on `r length(unique(crown_width_data2$spcd))` species.

Aaron and David previously determined that the 95th percentile of crown width (`cw`) was a useful approximation for maximum crown width (`mcw`).

We split the analysis in two phases:

1. Develop equation form (system) and initial parameter estimates by computing the 95th percentile `cw` for 0.1 inch diameter at breast height (`dbh`) classes for each species.
2. Fit the final model with quantile regression on the filtered data.


### Phase 1
#### Global Classed `mcw`

Below is a graph of `mcw` (approximated using species-specific 0.1-inch `dbh` classes' 95th percentile `cw`). The graph illustrates that over all species, crown width tends toward an asymptote.

```{r}
#| label: graph_global_mcw
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

crown_width_data2 |> 
    mutate( dbh_class=as.integer(dbh_in*10+0.5)/10 ) |> 
    group_by( spcd, common_name, dbh_class) |> 
    summarize( cw_95=quantile(cw_ft,0.95) ) |>
    ggplot( aes( dbh_class, cw_95 )) +
    geom_point( ) + 
    xlab( "DBH Class (0.1-inch bins)" ) + ylab( "95th percentile Crown Width (feet)" ) +
    ggtitle( "Global (all species) Maximum Crown Width (feet)" ) +
    geom_smooth()

```

We fit the filtered and classed data using @eq-gmcw:

$$ cw_{95} = \beta_0 dbhc^{\beta_1}$$ {#eq-gmcw}

where:

* $cw_{95}$ - 95th percentile crown width (feet) for species-specific 0.1-inch `dbh` class 
* $dbhc$ - 0.1-inch `dbh` class (inches)

The fit statistics are shown below with a residual graph. The global fit does not show serious residual trends across `dbh`, but there is a significant difference between conifers and hardwoods.

```{r}
#| label: fit_global_mcw
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

d <- crown_width_data2 |> 
    mutate( dbh_class=as.integer(dbh_in*10+0.5)/10 ) |> 
    group_by( type, spcd, common_name, dbh_class) |> 
    summarize( cw_95=quantile(cw_ft,0.95) ) 

gmcw_fit <- nls( cw_95~b0*dbh_class^b1, data=d, start=c(b0=1.5,b1=0.5), trace=F)
summary( gmcw_fit )

d |> ggplot( aes( dbh_class, -residuals(gmcw_fit) ) ) + 
    geom_point() + geom_abline( intercept = 0, slope=0.0 ) +
    geom_smooth() +
    theme(legend.position = "none") + 
    ylim( c(-50,50) ) +
    xlab( "DBH Class (0.1-inch bins)" ) + ylab( "95th percentile Crown Width Residual (pred-actual) (feet)" ) 

d |> ggplot( aes( type, -residuals(gmcw_fit) ) ) +
    geom_boxplot(notch=T, varwidth=T ) + geom_abline( intercept = 0, slope=0.0 ) +
    xlab( "" ) + ylab( "95th percentile Crown Width Residual (pred-actual) (feet)" ) 

    
```
\pagebreak

#### Global Classed `mcw` with Conifer/Hardwood Differentiation

We adjusted @eq-gmcw to add an indicator variable (`type` (1 if conifer, 0 if hardwood) to adjust $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$. We found that the
$\beta_0$ adjustment was not significant, so the resulting new equation is @eq-gmcw2:

$$ cw_{95} = \beta_0 dbhc^{(\beta_1 + \beta_{1a}type)}$$ {#eq-gmcw2}

where:

* $cw_{95}$ - 95th percentile crown width (feet) for species-specific 0.1-inch `dbh` class 
* $dbhc$ - 0.1-inch `dbh` class (inches)
* $type$ - 1 if conifer, 0 if hardwood


The fit statistics for @eq-gmcw2 are shown below with a residual graph. The new global fit does not show serious residual trends across `dbh`, and removes the difference between conifers and hardwoods. Looking at residuals at the species level reveals that there are species-level effects that need to be accounted for (see last graph in this section).


```{r}
#| label: fit_global_mcw2
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

d2 <- crown_width_data2 |>
    mutate( dbh_class=as.integer(dbh_in*10+0.5)/10 ) |> 
    group_by( type, spcd, common_name, dbh_class) |> 
    summarize( cw_95=quantile(cw_ft,0.95) ) 

gmcw_fit2 <- minpack.lm::nlsLM( cw_95~(b0)*dbh_class^(b1+b1a*(type=="Conifer")), data=d2, 
                                start=c(b0=6.375,b1=0.575682,b1a=-0.132076), trace=F )
summary( gmcw_fit2 )


d2 |> ggplot( aes( dbh_class, -residuals(gmcw_fit2) ) ) + 
    geom_point() + geom_abline( intercept = 0, slope=0.0 ) +
    geom_smooth() +
    theme(legend.position = "none") + 
    ylim( c(-50,50) ) +
    xlab( "DBH Class (0.1-inch bins)" ) + ylab( "95th percentile CW Residual (pred-actual) (feet)" ) +
    ggtitle( "MCW Equation using Species Type")

d2 |> ggplot( aes( type, -residuals(gmcw_fit2) ) ) +
    geom_boxplot(notch=T, varwidth=T ) + geom_abline( intercept = 0, slope=0.0 ) +
    xlab( "" ) + ylab( "95th percentile CW Residual (pred-actual) (feet)" ) +
    ggtitle( "MCW Equation using Species Type")


d2 |> ggplot( aes( dbh_class, -residuals(gmcw_fit2), color=as.factor(spcd) ) ) + 
    geom_point() + geom_abline( intercept = 0, slope=0.0 ) +
    geom_smooth() +
    ylim( c( -50,50 ) ) +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    xlab( "DBH Class (0.1-inch bins)" ) + ylab( "95th percentile CW Residual (pred-actual) (feet)" ) +
    ggtitle( "MCW Equation using Species Type", subtitle="Colored by Species")
    

```

\pagebreak

#### Global Classed `mcw` with Conifer/Hardwood Differentiation and Species-specific Adjustments

To maintain the global curve shape and stable estimates provided by @eq-gmcw2, we computed the mean ratio of @eq-gmcw2 predictions to $cw_{95}$ by species on the 0.1-inch `dbh` classed data. The graphs below show the residuals after the adjustment. The adjustments reduce the species-specific biases.

```{r}
#| label: fit_global_mcw3
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

d3 <- d2 |> ungroup() |> 
    mutate( mcw_hat = predict(gmcw_fit2), mcw_ratio = cw_95/mcw_hat ) |>
    group_by( spcd ) |>
    summarise( mean_ratio = mean( mcw_ratio ) ) |>
    inner_join( d2, by="spcd" ) |>
    mutate( mcw_hat = predict(gmcw_fit2), mcw_hat2 = mcw_hat*mean_ratio ) 

d3 |> ggplot( aes( dbh_class, mcw_hat2-cw_95, color=as.factor(spcd) ) ) + 
    geom_point() + geom_abline( intercept = 0, slope=0.0 ) +
    geom_smooth() +
    ylim( c( -50,50 ) ) +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    xlab( "DBH Class (0.1-inch bins)" ) + ylab( "95th percentile CW Residual (pred-actual) (feet)" ) +
    ggtitle( "MCW Equation using Species Level Adjustments")

d3 |> ggplot( aes( type, mcw_hat2-cw_95) ) + geom_boxplot( notch=T ) + 
    geom_abline( intercept = 0, slope = 0 ) + 
    xlab( "" ) + ylab( "95th percentile CW Residual (pred-actual) (feet)" ) +
    ggtitle( "MCW Equation using Species Level Adjustments")
    
```


\pagebreak

### Phase 2 
#### Parameter Estimates using Quantile Regression


Using the filtered `cw` data we fit @eq-gmcw2 to the individual tree data using quantile regression with a $\tau$ = 0.95. The predictions from the quantile regression were then used to compute species-level adjustment ratios. Those ratios were applied to the tree-level data.

The regression summary statistics for the quantile regression are shown below along with a table showing the adjusted $\beta_0$ parameter estimates by species.

```{r}
#| label: fit_global_mcw4
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false


# fit stage 1 model
mcw_fit <- quantreg::nlrq( cw_ft ~ b0*dbh_in^(b1+b1a*(type=="Conifer")), 
                           data=crown_width_data2, 
                           tau = 0.95,
                           start=c(b0=5.3247,b1=0.435,b1a=-0.1362), trace = F )

summary( mcw_fit)

# compute species level adjustments
ratios <- crown_width_data2 |> ungroup() |> 
    mutate( mcw_hat = predict(mcw_fit), dbh_class=as.integer(dbh_in*10+0.5)/10 ) |>
    group_by( spcd, dbh_class ) |>
    summarize( cw_95=quantile(cw_ft,0.95), mean_mcw_hat=mean(mcw_hat), mcw_ratio=cw_95/mean_mcw_hat ) |>
    summarise( mean_ratio = mean( mcw_ratio ) ) |> ungroup() |>
    group_by( spcd ) |>
    summarize( mean_ratio = mean(mean_ratio) )

cw_data2 <- crown_width_data2 |> ungroup() |> 
    mutate( mcw_hat = predict(mcw_fit), dbh_class=as.integer(dbh_in*10+0.5)/10 ) |>
    group_by( type, spcd, dbh_class ) |>
    summarize( cw_95=quantile(cw_ft,0.95), mean_mcw_hat=mean(mcw_hat) ) |>
    inner_join( ratios, by="spcd" ) |>
    mutate( adj_mcw_hat=mean_mcw_hat*mean_ratio ) 

cw_data2 |>
    ggplot( aes( dbh_class, adj_mcw_hat-cw_95, color=as.factor(spcd) ) ) + 
    geom_point() + geom_abline( intercept = 0, slope=0.0 ) +
    geom_smooth() +
    ylim( c( -50,50 ) ) +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    xlab( "DBH Class (inches)" ) + ylab( "Maximum CW Residual (pred-actual) (feet)" ) +
    ggtitle( "Quantile Regression MCW Equation using Species Level Adjustments")

cw_data2 |> ggplot( aes( type, adj_mcw_hat-cw_95 ) ) + geom_boxplot( notch=T ) +
    geom_abline( intercept = 0, slope = 0 ) +
    xlab( "" ) + ylab( "Maximum CW Residual (pred-actual) (feet)" ) +
    ggtitle( "Quantile Regression MCW Equation using Species Level Adjustments")


knitr::kable( ratios |> mutate( b0adj=mcw_fit$m$getPars()[1] * mean_ratio ),
              col.names = c("spcd","adjustment ratio", "b0_adj"),
              caption = "Adjusted b0 Parameters" )


parms <- ratios |> mutate( b0adj=mcw_fit$m$getPars()[1] * mean_ratio, b1 = mcw_fit$m$getPars()[2], b1a = mcw_fit$m$getPars()[3] ) |>
    select( -mean_ratio )

saveRDS( parms, file=paste0( rds_path, "mcw_parms.RDS") )
```
### Equation Performance

Below is a graph of equation predictions by species.


```{r}
#| label: equation_performance
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

cw_data2 |> ggplot( aes( dbh_class, adj_mcw_hat, linetype = type, color=as.factor(spcd) ) ) + 
    geom_line() + 
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dotted")) +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    xlab( "DBH (inches)" ) + ylab( "Predicted Maximum Crown Width (feet)" ) +
    ggtitle( "Quantile Regression MCW Equation using Species Level Adjustments",
             subtitle="Colored by Species (Conifer=solid, Hardwood=Dotted")

```
## Conclusion

The system developed above accounts for species-level variation in `cw` without sacrificing biologically meaningful equation performance. It is unbiased against the fitting data. Generally, hardwoods have wider crowns than conifers. 

The system does produce some high predicted crown widths that should be investigated.
